here the concern is empirical (does the checklist cover the discriminative features?)","The expert's intuition is not necessarily the same as Polanyi's tacit knowledge\u2014it may be explicit knowledge applied rapidly"],"overturn_conditions":["Empirical demonstration that all discriminative features for the task are articulable and includable in a checklist","Evidence that expert intuition does not outperform checklist-guided non-experts on tacit-feature cases","Proof that non-expert panel members can access tacit features when the checklist is silent, rather than defaulting to checklist-based heuristics"],"shared_structure":["Polanyi's tacit knowledge vs. articulable rules maps to expert intuition vs. explicit checklist","The checklist's explicitness is its weakness: it excludes tacit features by definition","Objectively verifiable outcomes do not imply that the features determining the outcome are articulable"],"source_memory_refs":["SRC_006"],"transfer_claims":["Tacit feature recognition is a source of expert advantage that checklists cannot replicate","Systematic panel failure on tacit-feature items within a single evaluation demonstrates causal checklist inadequacy","The distinction between reliability loss from checklist inadequacy vs. panel compliance is made by item-level analysis partitioned by checklist-feature sufficiency"]},"claim":"The claim is false: a single domain expert relying on intuition will, on average, produce more reliable judgments than a panel of trained non-experts following an explicit checklist for tasks with objectively verifiable outcomes, because expertise involves tacit feature recognition that checklists systematically exclude. The single evaluation distinguishes genuine reliability loss in the panel from mere checklist inadequacy by comparing error profiles on items where the checklist's specified features are ambiguous or absent: if the panel fails systematically on these items while the expert succeeds, the checklist is causally responsible for the reliability gap, not the panel's compliance behavior.","counterconditions":[{"case":"The task domain has no tacit discriminative features\u2014every correct classification can be achieved via articulable features alone","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The expert's intuition is no better than chance on tacit-feature cases, meaning the expert's advantage is solely in articulable knowledge the checklist omits","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The checklist is dynamically adaptive, allowing panel members to flag items where checklist features are insufficient and defer to expert judgment","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Domain expertise is not merely a larger checklist; it includes tacit pattern recognition that operates on features the expert cannot articulate. An explicit checklist, by definition, captures only articulable features. For objectively verifiable outcomes, cases where the discriminative feature is tacit (perceptual, gestalt, or configural) will be systematically misclassified by the panel but potentially correctly classified by the expert. The checklist forces panel members to ignore their own nascent tacit recognition in favor of articulable criteria, destroying signal. The single-evaluation test: partition items by whether the checklist's specified features are sufficient for correct classification. If the panel underperforms the expert specifically on items where checklist features are ambiguous, this demonstrates that checklist constraint is causally reducing reliability, not merely failing to help.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
